Question: Is it possible for animals to create hybrids with other species, regardless of whether they have a common ancestor?
Old_Answer: Every single thing on Earth has a common ancestor. We all descend from LUCA (the Last Universal Common Ancestor). It’s only a question of how far back in time that ancestor lived. Species that can hybridize within the same Genus are common. Species that can hybridize with members of another genus are less common, but there are definitely a good number of them. Species that can hybridize with a member of a higher clade (above the level of Genus) are pretty rare. The less closely related species are, the more likely it is that their genes won’t line up correctly to create a viable organism. (Helmeted Guinea Fowl (Numididae Numida meleagris) crossed with Domestic Chicken (Phasianidae Gallus gallus domesticus. These birds are in different Linnaean Families/clades above the level of Genus. As you can see, the hybrid offspring are healthy, and look like what they are - half chicken, half guinea fowl).
Answer_with_writing_sample: Yes, it is indeed possible for animals to create hybrids with other species, even if they do not share a recent common ancestor. This phenomenon is generally more common within closely related species, which can produce viable hybrids due to their similar genetic makeup. An excellent example of this is the mule, a hybrid between a horse and a donkey. While these two species diverged millions of years ago, their genetic compatibility allows for the creation of a sterile offspring. However, hybridization can also occur between more distantly related species through mechanisms like polyploidy, where the number of chromosomes doubles, allowing for new species to emerge rapidly. For instance, many plants exhibit this ability, and some researchers have observed instances of hybridization in certain fish and amphibians that are not closely related, often in response to environmental changes. It's important to understand that hybridization can lead to a wealth of genetic diversity, but it also raises questions about the integrity and conservation of species. As hybrids often have mixed traits from their parent species, they may possess unique adaptations that allow them to thrive in particular ecological niches. However, this can sometimes result in competitive disadvantages or challenges in reproduction, leading to potential threats to the parent species. Therefore, the possibility of hybridization reflects the intricate interplay of genetics, evolution, and ecology, showcasing nature's remarkable ability to adapt and innovate, even across species boundaries.

Answer_with_full_information: Yes, it is indeed possible for animals to create hybrids with other species, even when they do not share a recent common ancestor. Question: Why do evolutionists prefer to pick on the bonobos for comparison with humans, instead of the more intelligent chimpanzees?
Old_Answer: First, there is no such thing as an ‘evolutionist.’ That’s a term that implies that acceptance of settled science is some sort of belief system or that there is some question about evolutionary theory. That is not the case. There are people who accept science, and science-deniers. Science denial is irrational. There is no need for special names for people who accept settled science based on which science they accept. Presumably, if they accept settled science on evolution, they accept settled science on everything else, too. lol. I think part of the issue stems from the fact that in common language, a theory is a speculation - a guess. But scientific terms have different definitions, and the term ‘theory’ in science means ‘an explanation for observed facts which is thoroughly supported by ample evidence, and has no contradictory evidence against it.’ First, a hypothesis is proposed - an explanation for facts we have observed. Then the hypothesis is rigorously tested, and evidence is collected. If the evidence all supports the hypothesis, and none disproves it, then it becomes a theory. Once the body of evidence becomes truly overwhelming and massive, then we say that it is a Proven Theory. Evolutionary theory is a proven theory - it is the closest that science can ever come to producing an absolute truth. There are no remaining doubts about it. Not even one. There is no evidence that does not support it. None at all. So, if you want to question accepted science, then you need to actual do science and research. You need to present material facts that contradict the hypothesis or theory, and they need to have been collected using rational, rigorous methods. You need to actually scientifically DISPROVE a theory in order to effectively overturn it. Anything else is meaningless nonsense; irrational behavior based in pretending that reality is not what it is. And no, believing someone else who said they did the work is not sufficient. You have to actually explore and understand their work, and it has to have been duplicated and verified. No one takes anyone at their word. Belief should never have a role to play in any of this. Science is about using a rational method to explore reality and find out what it really is. It does not include faith/absolute certainty, ever. I wanted to make this clear before moving on to the next part of your question, because you went on to state a couple more things that weren’t true. First you said that scientists (this is what you really meant) choose to compare humans and bonobos rather than humans and chimps. This is simply not true. Both species are compared to humans, and their cognition is studied to aid our understanding of our own evolution. Next, you said that chimpanzees are more intelligent than bonobos. This is also not true. Intelligence is not all one thing, and these two species have different intellectual strengths and weaknesses from each other, as well as from us. Bonobos are far more skilled at solving tasks that relate to the theory of mind and social causality, while chimps are more skilled at solving tasks that relate to tool use and physical causality. In short, bonobos are better at knowing themselves and others, while chimps are better at understanding physics. Chimpanzees are far more aggressive than bonobos, and this holds them back to some degree. They are, in fact, more aggressive than humans, having a significantly higher rate of reactive aggression. Bonobos, conversely, are about equal to humans in reactive aggression. Chimps also have a higher rate of proactive aggression than humans do, but humans have a higher rate of proactive aggression than Bonobos. To put this into perspective, a chimp is smart enough to sharpen a stick to stab you with because you made him angry by grinning at him. And he’ll do it, too. lol. A bonobo is smart enough to understand that you aren’t a bonobo and your body language is different from his, so he doesn’t have any reason to be angry that you grinned at him. Which one is ‘smarter?’ I will also leave you with the fact that humans are not superior in all areas of cognition to our closest relatives. As I pointed out, cognition is not all one thing. And we don’t win in every area. Chimpanzees wipe the floor with us in tests of working memory. No contest. Even when we have time to practice, they still beat us. They are simply BETTER at noting where things are, exactly, and remembering it five minutes later when they can’t see those things anymore. As for bonobos - a bonobo was able to recognize both her sister and her nephew in photographs after not having seen either one for 26 years, which is the longest term social memory documented in a non-human animal. (I don’t think the working memory of bonobos has been tested, yet). So, we have very good reasons to study the cognitive abilities of both species, as an aid to understanding how various parts of the brain work, and how our own cognitive arrangement likely evolved.
